fields.hint: npm, Vite and an Express server are all written in JavaScript; ask where each one runs when you use it.
fields.explanation: Node runs JavaScript directly on a machine — a server, a laptop, a CI runner — with no browser involved; that is how npm, Vite and an Express server work. It does not run inside a browser tab, an HTML page or a mobile web view; those environments bring their own JavaScript engines. Node can also run a script piped in on stdin.

fields.explanation: Node’s core APIs start an operation, return immediately, and deliver the result later through a callback, promise or event — non-blocking, event-driven I/O — so one thread keeps serving other work while the disk or network is busy. Node also offers blocking *Sync variants, but they are the exception; it does not dedicate a thread to each connection, and it does not spin polling for results: libuv sleeps until the operating system (or, for file reads, its thread pool) reports completion.

fields.explanation: Node caches each module by resolved filename in `require.cache`: the module code runs once and every later `require()` returns the same exports object, in every environment and for user modules as well as core modules. Deleting the cache entry forces a fresh load (rarely a good idea), and a specifier that resolves to a different filename (a different letter case on a case-insensitive file system, or a second copy inside another node_modules folder) produces a separate instance.

fields.explanation: `__dirname` is the absolute path of the directory containing the current CommonJS module file, unaffected by where the process was launched (that is `process.cwd()`); the file’s own path is `__filename`, and Node has no notion of a project root. In ES modules `__dirname` is not defined at all (reading it throws a ReferenceError); use `import.meta.dirname` (Node 20.11+, stable since 22.16) instead.

fields.explanation: await suspends the async function (not the whole process) until the awaited promise resolves or rejects. The rest of the program keeps running while it is suspended, on the same thread: nothing is blocked, no new thread appears, and awaiting a promise never cancels it. If the promise rejects, the await throws, so wrap it in try/catch.

fields.explanation: A rejected promise throws at the await, so a try/catch around it (or around a group of awaits) receives the error and lets the function recover or rethrow; calling .catch() on the promise is an equally valid alternative. The awaited value is never an Error object on failure, because the code after the await does not run; the function you await hands back a promise rather than reporting errors through a callback; and finally runs cleanup but does not catch anything.
